messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas had been a hotel manager for thirty years, a man who prided himself on knowing every corridor, every guest, every staff member’s name. The night he was mugged, the hallway he walked each evening with the key card to the executive lounge was suddenly an alley of strangers. A young man in a hoodie appeared from the shadows, demanded Thomas’s wallet, and when Thomas refused to give it up, the attacker lunged with a knife. The confrontation ended with Thomas’s wallet in the man’s hand and a bruised thumb, but the damage was not just physical. Thomas felt the sting of humiliation the instant he realized he had been taken in his own establishment, the feeling that his professional identity had been publicly stripped away. In the days that followed he began to think that people could not be trusted; that the world, once a place of hospitality and routine, was now a dangerous arena. Those negative appraisals—mistrust, humiliation, a world in which danger lurked—were the seeds that sprouted his constant state of alertness. From that point onward, Thomas’s perception of threat dominated his thoughts. The belief that every stranger might want his wallet or his valuables meant that he was always super‑alert, constantly scanning. He became hypervigilant; a single sound could set his heart racing, and he reacted with alarm when a colleague touched his arm for the first time in months. Even in the quiet of his own home, he felt a persistent need to check that every door was locked, every window was secure, and he lay awake in the dark, listening to the faint creak of the floorboards as if a thief could be listening too. When he returned to the hotel each morning, those heightened threat perceptions turned the ordinary into potential danger. A guest walking past the reception desk would trigger a flinch; a man in a business suit walking past the elevators would make Thomas’s eyes flicker to the door as if expecting a threat. The smell of alcohol coming from the staff lounge or the bar during a busy evening became a cue that danger might be imminent. Loud noises—whether a sudden burst of laughter in the dining room or the clatter of plates—would set his hands trembling, and he would pause in the doorway, heart hammering, before he could speak to a guest. The triggers he was now sensitive to were not random; they were the manifestations of the threat state that his negative appraisals had cemented. Whenever a suspicious face appeared or the scent of alcohol drifted through the hallway, Thomas’s hypervigilance made him see danger where it had not been before, and his body responded with a startle to touch that kept him perpetually on edge. The cycle tightened further as Thomas began to avoid the very situations that might help him feel safe. He began to refuse to stay late when the bar was busy, to keep his staff’s access to the guest rooms restricted, and to ask his wife to stay out of the hotel after hours. He stopped participating in staff meetings that were held in the lounge, fearing the alcohol smell and the loud conversations. In the evenings, he would not go to the local pub with friends because he imagined the people might act suspiciously or that a stranger might approach him on the sidewalk. Each avoidance solidified his perception of the world as unsafe and increased his sense of humiliation for being unable to engage normally. The hypervigilant, startle‑prone Thomas found himself unable to relax even when he was at home, constantly on guard, feeling the weight of his past event on every creak and every scent. Now, at the age of sixty‑seven, Thomas sits in a therapist’s office, eyes darting as he speaks of the mugging. He tells the therapist that he feels “sick” whenever someone near him appears uneasy, and that the smell of beer makes him feel as if someone is plotting to take his life. He admits that he has begun to withdraw from his wife’s visits to the hotel, afraid that she might witness his erratic behavior or that someone else might see him as a target. His marriage, once a source of comfort, has become a source of anxiety because he cannot trust his partner’s presence to calm him. The fear that he will once again be humiliated or robbed has kept him from sleeping peacefully, and his exhaustion has made him less efficient at managing his staff. When he looks at the ledger of his hotel, he sees not only numbers but a ledger of threats that he must constantly monitor. Thomas’s most urgent hope is to feel safe again—both in the corridors of the hotel he manages and in his own home. His greatest fear is that one day the triggers he has become attuned to will strike again, that another assault will bring his world back to that night in the hallway, and that his reputation as a competent, trustworthy manager will crumble. It is this desperate longing for safety and stability that finally led him to seek help, hoping that the weight of the negative appraisals will loosen and that the constant threat will no longer dictate every moment of his life.
